column4: The section's lexical image of the sky as what covers above extends downward through cloud and rain to pasture; this verse joins the sky as a canopy, water sent down, and fruit brought out from earth.
This sign sequence places winds, clouds held between sky and earth, rain, and revived land together, matching the section's vertical passage from cloud to living growth.
The section develops weak lightning at cloud edges; this rainstorm parable explicitly stages rain from the sky, darkness, thunder, and lightning, though its primary point is people in doubt.
The verse's برق nearly snatches sight: it gives the section's faint cloud-edge flash a brighter storm counterpart and makes visibility itself unstable.
The verse moves from water sent down to varied plants, green growth, grain, dates, and ripening fruit, a close Qur'anic staging of rain bringing vegetation out.

The passage sends winds before mercy, carries heavy clouds to a dead land, sends rain, brings out fruit, and compares this to bringing out the dead; it gathers the section's full rain-to-growth-to-resurrection chain.
The section defines المرعى as plant, place, and grazing; this adjacent verse says good land yields its vegetation by its Lord's permission, while poor land yields little.
The verse makes worldly life a rain-fed crop that flourishes, then is harvested away as if it had not flourished yesterday, sharpening the section's green-to-debris arc.
The verse contrasts gardens, crops, and date palms watered by one water but yielding differently, a specific parallel to the section's patchy first growth and varied pasture.
The section's root خ ف ي is given a weak-flash sense at cloud edges; this verse explicitly joins lightning that evokes fear and hope to heavy clouds.

The section's غثاء is flood-carried vegetation piled together; here floodwater carries زبدًا that passes away while what benefits people remains, joining torrent residue to the distinction between passing and lasting.
The section names a southern wind that sustains and drives clouds; this verse gives winds a concrete role in pollination and then connects them to water sent down.
This verse says rainwater gives drink and produces vegetation for grazing, directly linking rain to pasture and animal feeding.
The verse names crops, olives, palms, grapes, and fruits grown by the rain, widening the same provision scene from pasture to harvest.
The verse says God revives the earth after its death with rain; it gives Qur'anic form to the section's plant journey from dead soil to living growth.
The section sets the plant's short life beside what is better and more abiding; this verse says what people have runs out while what is with God remains.
The garden story named immediately before the section's worldly-life parable begins with two gardens of vines, palms, and crops, the lush cultivated scene that the next image makes transient.
The verse says both gardens yield their produce and a river runs between them, supplying the abundance that makes the later collapse meaningful.
The owner enters his garden while wronging himself and says he does not think it will ever perish; the section's plant cycle directly overturns that confidence.
The garden owner doubts the Hour and his return to his Lord, making the section's temporary vegetation and lasting Hereafter distinction especially pointed.
The companion warns that a calamity from heaven could strike the garden and leave it bare and slippery, a destructive reversal of rain-fed flourishing.
The warning that the garden's water may sink away supplies the opposite boundary to the section's rain that makes pasture emerge.
The garden's produce is destroyed and its owner wrings his hands over what he spent; this is a concrete human loss beside the section's natural conversion of green growth to debris.
The verse explicitly compares worldly life to rain from heaven: earth's growth becomes dry fragments scattered by winds, almost exactly the section's plant-to-debris sequence.
The section links أبقى to what endures; this verse names the lasting good deeds as better with one's Lord than the rain-grown life that vanishes.
The source section uses the root خ ف ي for lightning that glimmers faintly at a cloud's edge; this verse uses أَخْفَى for what is more concealed, a lexical boundary between faintly seen and hidden.
This is Pharaoh's question, “Who is your Lord, Moses?”; the section cites it to frame Moses' answer about the Lord who creates, guides, and brings forth plants in 20:50 and 20:53.
The answer names the Lord as the one who gives each thing its form and then guides it, joining the section's Lord-language to the ordered emergence of pasture.
The verse describes earth spread out, water sent down, and varied plants brought forth; the source section's root خ ر ج for extracting vegetation is explicit here.
This continuation tells people to eat and pasture their cattle, directly activating the section's threefold sense of المرعى as vegetation, grazing place, and grazing.
The verse says humans are created from earth, returned to it, and brought out again, extending the plant's earth-to-emergence cycle to resurrection.
The verse says the condemned person neither dies nor lives in the Fire, the exact boundary the section sets against a plant's living and dead phases.
The verse joins the heavens and earth being separated with every living thing made from water, making water the source of life in the section's rain-and-pasture image.
The barren earth receives water, stirs, swells, and grows varied plants; the verse then compares this revival to human resurrection.
This verse sends down water from the sky in measure and settles it in the earth, while warning that it could be taken away; it frames the rain on which pasture depends.
This continuation brings forth gardens of dates and grapes and other fruits, a specific harvest following the measured water.
The source section defines غثاء as plant gathered and carried by a flood; this verse uses غثاء for a people after the cry, transferring the plant's debris image to a community.
The verse describes clouds joined and piled into layers, rain emerging through them, and lightning; it supplies the cloud-and-flash scene developed by the section.
This verse sends winds as heralds before mercy and sends down purifying water from the sky, matching the section's wind, cloud, and rain sequence.
The water revives a dead land and gives drink to people and animals; its life-giving rain stands against the section's later dry debris.
The verse asks who sends water down and brings forth gardens, then says people cannot make their trees grow; it makes vegetation's emergence a sign of the Lord's agency.
The verse calls worldly gifts adornment and says what is with God is better and more abiding, echoing the section's contrast between temporary green growth and what remains.
The verse joins rain from the sky to earth revived after death, then asks who does this; it is a direct formulation of the section's rain-to-life pattern.
The verse says the living comes from the dead and the dead from the living, and that earth is revived after death, directly stating the cycle the section makes visible in pasture.
The verse links lightning that raises fear and hope to rain and earth revived after death, combining the section's faint flash with its rain-grown vegetation.
This verse calls winds glad tidings of mercy and of ships seeking provision; it prepares the cloud-and-rain action in 30:48 that the section's image develops.
The verse says winds drive clouds, which spread and pile up, then rain emerges; this directly stages the section's cloud being carried to the land.
This verse describes people's despair before rain arrives; the following 30:50 turns to the traces of mercy and revived earth, completing the weather reversal.
The command to look at the traces of God's mercy points to the earth revived after death; this matches the source section's first-rain mark on the land and its green return.
The verse joins rain sent down from the sky to the growth of every noble kind of plant, a compact version of the section's vertical rain-to-pasture column.
The verse drives water to barren land and brings out crops eaten by people and their grazing animals, directly joining soil, rain, and pasture.
The verse describes winds driving clouds to dead land and reviving earth after its death, then names resurrection; it closely parallels the section's weather and plant cycle.
The verse says water from the sky brings fruits of varied colors; this gives a Qur'anic color counterpart to the section's dark-green-to-black description of أَحْوَى.
The dead earth is a sign: God revives it and brings grain from it for food, matching the section's emergence of pasture from soil.
This continuation places date palms and grape gardens in the revived land, specifying the produce that follows the grain.
The verse asks whether people made these gardens grow or God did, tying the crop scene to the section's Lord as giver and grower.

The verse sends water down, brings out crops of varied colors, then turns them yellow and into debris; جَعَلَهُ in the source section likewise names the plant's change of state, and this verse ends with a reminder.
The verse points to earth that is subdued, then stirs and grows when water descends; its revival is called a sign of God's power.
The verse sends rain after people have despaired and spreads mercy, a specific reversal from withheld water to renewed life.
The verse sends down water from the sky in due measure, revives a dead town, and says people will be brought out likewise; it joins measured rain to resurrection.
The verse groups night and day, rain that revives earth after death, and winds as signs, bringing together several elements of the section's weather cycle.
The people mistake an approaching cloud for rain, but it is a painful wind; this reverses the section's life-giving cloud and rain expectation.
The wind destroys everything by its Lord's command, a specific boundary to the section's cloud as the source of pasture and growth.
The verse describes blessed rain, gardens, and grain for harvest, a direct rain-to-food counterpart to the pasture emergence in the section.
This continuation adds tall date palms with layered fruit, showing the rain's yield in a concrete plant form.
The verse says rain revives a dead land and calls resurrection “the خروج”; it explicitly moves from plant revival to the dead being brought out.
The source section defines أَحْوَى as darkened from green; this verse calls two gardens مُدْهَامَّتَان, a Qur'anic image of greenery so dense it appears dark.
The verse asks people to consider what they sow, introducing a crop cycle whose growth the next verse assigns to God.
The question “Are you the growers, or are We?” makes plant emergence depend on divine agency, as in the section's Lord and pasture.
The verse says God could make the crop حُطَامًا; the source section's غثاء is the flood-gathered dry plant residue, a close parallel in the crop's broken end.
The following lament says the crop leaves them in debt, showing the human loss after the possible crop failure in 56:65.
This continuation says they have been deprived, completing the crop-failure outcome that contrasts with pasture as provision.
The verse asks who sends down drinking water from rainclouds, returning directly to the water source of the section's vegetation.
The verse asks whether people or God send the rainwater, underscoring the giver behind the section's rain-fed growth.
The verse says God could make the water bitter; this is a specific reversal of rain as life-giving water.
The verse says God gives life to earth after its death and makes the signs clear, a concise statement of the section's dead-soil-to-green motif.
The verse makes worldly life a rain-fed crop that grows, yellows, and becomes حُطَامًا; it explicitly frames the plant's decay as a reminder of passing life.

The source section gives اسم an attested alternative derivation from وسم and pictures first rain marking earth with plants; this verse uses سَنَسِمُهُ for branding a person, a distant but concrete mark-image rather than a shared root identity.
The verse says God caused people to grow from earth like a plant, giving the section's plant emergence a direct human counterpart.
This continuation says people return to earth and are brought out again, completing the human cycle beside 71:17's growth from earth.
The verse says God brought out the earth's water and pasture; the source section's مرعى carries vegetation, pasture-place, and grazing, all concentrated here.
This verse says the water, pasture, and mountains are provision for people and their livestock, completing the pasture's role as sustenance.
The command to consider food introduces the sequence in 80:25–32, where rain, split earth, grain, fruit, pasture, and provision explain what sustains life.
The verse says water is poured down, giving the rain source for the food sequence that follows.
The earth is split open after the rain, a concrete counterpart to the section's vegetation being brought out from soil.
The next product is grain, specifying one form of the earth's growth.
This continuation names grapes among the growth brought out of earth.
The verse adds olives and date palms to the rain-fed plant sequence.
The sequence then names dense gardens, the cultivated abundance behind the food image.
The verse names fruit and أَبًّا; the latter is pasture or fodder, directly meeting the section's plant-and-grazing sense of مرعى.
This closing verse calls the fruit and pasture provision for people and their livestock, making the pasture's grazing function explicit.
The verse lists crops and livestock among the adornments of worldly life, a concrete link between the section's pasture imagery and its contrast with what lasts.
The verse sends water from heaven and brings out fruits as provision, a direct rain-to-harvest formulation alongside the section's pasture.
The verse contrasts worldly enjoyment with provision from one's Lord that is better and أبقى; the source section uses the same root أبقى to frame what outlasts the plant's short life.
The verse says abundant rain is sent from clouds, followed by grain and gardens in 78:15–16; it is another compact rain-to-harvest scene.
This adjacent verse names grain and vegetation brought forth by the abundant rain in 78:14.
The following verse adds lush gardens to the grain and vegetation sequence begun in 78:14.

The verse's seed yields seven ears, a specific image of growth multiplying from what is sown; this adds a crop-growth parallel to the section's plant emerging from earth, though its point is charitable giving.
The verse pictures a fertile garden on a height receiving heavy rain or drizzle and yielding fruit, a specific soil-and-rain counterpart to the section's pasture emerging under rain.

The verse's flourishing garden is struck by a fiery whirlwind and burned; this is a concrete reversal of the section's rain-fed green growth, though the cause is sudden fire rather than natural drying.
This preceding verse spreads the earth and names rivers and paired fruits; it supplies the earth-and-fruit setting continued by 13:4's gardens and crops.
The good word is compared to a good tree with firm roots and branches reaching skyward, joining the section's rooted emergence to its vertical sky-to-pasture image.
The tree yields fruit by its Lord's permission; this gives a recurring, sustained counterpart to the section's pasture and its root-family image of a cloud that nurtures plants.
The bad word is compared to a tree uprooted from the earth with no stability, a specific plant reversal beside the section's growth from soil and its later debris.
The verse says rain from the sky makes the earth green, a direct compact formulation of the section's cloud-to-rain-to-pasture scene.
This next verse adds the olive tree of Mount Sinai, yielding oil and food, to the date, grape, and garden produce named in 23:19.

The word نُرَبِّكَ is from the source section's root ر ب ب in the explicit nurturing sense: Pharaoh says he raised Moses as a child. The section links that root-family to a cloud that nurtures plants, extending the sustaining image to human upbringing.

This verse says that when God calls people from the earth they come forth; the source section's root خ ر ج describes pasture brought out from earth, and here the same extraction image points to resurrection.
After 30:50 describes revived earth, this verse presents a wind and something seen yellow; it gives the rain-revived scene its specific yellowing reversal.
The verse answers who can revive decayed bones: the one who created them first. Its contribution is the resurrection claim, followed in 36:80 by a green-tree-and-fire sign.
The verse asks who made the tree from which people kindle fire; green vegetation thus yields fire, joining the section's pasture cycle to the later Fire image in Surah 87.
The verse says herbs and trees prostrate; alongside Surah 87's opening command to glorify the Most High, it makes vegetation itself part of the worship scene.
This adjacent verse says the heaven was raised and balance set, carrying the sky-and-earth frame of 55:6 into the section's vertical image from above to pasture.
The passage next says the earth was laid out for living creatures, giving the ground beneath the section's emerging pasture its place in the created order.
This continuation names fruit and date palms, extending the earth's produce scene beyond the pasture.
The verse adds grain and fragrant plants, a specific crop-and-herb counterpart to the section's grass and grazing.
The two gardens of Paradise have gushing springs, a lasting garden scene that marks a boundary against the section's pasture that dries and is carried away.
This garden passage names fruit, date palms, and pomegranates; it continues the unwithering produce scene begun in 55:64.

After the surah's images of prostrating plants, raised heaven, earth, fruit, and dark gardens, this closing verse blesses the name of the Lord, echoing the section's opening “name of your Lord” across a botanical and celestial sequence.
The verse asks people to consider the fire they kindle; it opens the adjacent creation passage in which 56:72 identifies the tree from which fire is made.
The verse asks who made the tree that supplies kindling; it specifically joins plant growth to fire, a reversal of the section's green pasture and a bridge to Surah 87's Fire.
The continuation calls that fire a reminder and provision for travelers, joining the tree-to-fire image to the section's movement from the plant cycle toward reminder.
The verse says the people of the Fire have only thorny ضَرِيع for food; this is a specific boundary to the section's pasture as grazing and provision.
The next verse says that food neither nourishes nor relieves hunger, contrasting the pasture's sustaining growth with the Fire's barren provision.
